title: Teaching prayer
hook: a granddaughter on his shoulder, all the way through the prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, khitan, and your line: the way of ibrahim. Did a custom you don't share come up, and did you ask? Today, a parent, a child, and the prayer between them. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-four.

A man stands in prayer with a little girl up on his shoulder. When he goes down to prostrate, he sets her gently on the floor. When he stands up again, he lifts her back up. Sahih al-Bukhari tells it, in paraphrase: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, prayed while carrying his granddaughter Umamah, the daughter of his daughter Zaynab. No lecture about prayer. Just a child, riding along through it, watching every movement from up close. Today: how a child learns to pray.
screen: `A GIRL ON HIS SHOULDER.` → `DOWN TO PROSTRATE.` → `UP AGAIN WHEN HE STANDS.`

segments.voice: Start with the instruction people quote. In Sunan Abu Dawud, in paraphrase, the Prophet said: command your children to pray when they are seven years old. The same hadith goes on to speak of the age of ten with firmer words, and scholars discuss what that firmness should and shouldn't mean. But notice the order. Seven comes first, three years before the firmer words. A child isn't asked to pray as an adult does. They're given time to grow into it. Second, the Qur'an puts this in a parent's mouth. In surah Luqman, a wise father advises his son, and when he comes to prayer, in Pickthall's translation, he says: "O my dear son! Establish worship." My dear son. The words are tender before they're firm. Third, the Prophet didn't treat a child as an interruption. Umamah on his shoulder. Down when he prostrates. Up when he stands. Every movement of the prayer, seen from the closest seat in the room. Arabic has a word for what he was being: a qudwah, an example to follow. A child copies the bow before understanding it, and learns the words from hearing them said nearby. Fourth, the line that ties it together. The Qur'an tells the Prophet, in Pickthall's words: "And enjoin upon thy people worship, and be constant therein." Enjoin, and be constant. Tell others, and keep doing it yourself. That's today's line. The instruction and the example travel together, and without the example, the instruction has nothing to point to.
screen: `PRAY AT SEVEN: YEARS TO GROW INTO IT.` · `O MY DEAR SON! ESTABLISH WORSHIP.` · `UMAMAH ON HIS SHOULDER.` · `ENJOIN IT, AND BE CONSTANT.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray with a child, or near one. Settle, and breathe. If you pray and there's a child in your life, think of the next prayer you could let them watch, or join, or just sit beside. No correcting. Just doing it where they can see. If there's no child near you, remember the first person you watched do something devoted: pray, read, give, light a candle. Let the picture be someone small watching someone bigger, unhurried, and what the small one took away. The bell holds the time.
Teaching prayer. Children are told to pray from seven, and they learn it beside someone who prays. Today's word.
Your line: teach by praying. Today, let one good thing you do be seen by someone younger, without a speech. Tomorrow, the first khatm. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Muslim parents who follow the hadith in Abu Dawud begin teaching children the prayer around the age of seven, and children often learn it by praying beside their parents at home and in the mosque.

fork.setup: you're praying with your small granddaughter up on your shoulder. it's time to go down and prostrate. what do you do?
options: stop the prayer and hand her to someone.
set her down gently, and lift her again when you stand.
fork.reveal: that's what Bukhari reports: down when he prostrated, up when he stood. the child stayed, and watched the whole prayer.

original.note: Arabic: an example to follow, a model.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lesson plan for kids.
what it means: children grow into prayer from seven, mostly by watching and joining the people who pray beside them.
what a scholar hears: Abu Dawud's hadith on seven and ten, read beside Luqman 31:17, 20:132's 'enjoin… and be constant', and Bukhari's report of Umamah carried in prayer.
